summary:
Arunāchal Pradesh stands under India's national framework on gender recognition, criminal law and police conduct, and that framework is what a trans visitor to the state should be assessed against. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the self-identification route of the 2019 law.

Legal recognition is now restricted to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and requires medical certification: medical boards and district authorities must certify whether gender-affirming surgery has been performed. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 26 March 2026, states that the amendment reverses the position set by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 ruling on gender identity.

The amendment adds offences including up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warns that the provision could criminalise the support networks trans people rely on. Coverage under the recognition scheme is narrow in practice: of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, only about 32,500 hold identity cards, against an estimated two million transgender people in India.

Presidential assent was pending as of late March 2026. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling the removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling. The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics warn that it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people, and rights activists describe the amendment as an attack on the right to exist.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Court has interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership in India, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student was stopped at Chennai International Airport by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Access to care and facilities is largely set at state level. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.
tangentialFactors:
Several Indian states run transgender welfare boards that coordinate housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions; Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha are the documented examples, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. A visitor moving between states may therefore encounter materially different access to surgery, pensions and housing support than in Arunāchal Pradesh.

Intersex minors remain at risk across the country. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

The 2026 amendment's trajectory is contested at the highest level: a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel sought withdrawal of the bill, and Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign it, while the government frames the narrower recognition test as an expansion of welfare access and trafficking protection.
localsOnly:
Residents of Arunāchal Pradesh are assessed under the amended national recognition scheme, which requires medical certification by medical boards and district authorities rather than self-declaration, and which limits recognition to hijra, kinner and intersex categories. Only about 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender people in India hold identity cards, so documentation status is the practical determinant of access to schemes.

Transition-related healthcare is covered nationally under the Ayushman Bharat scheme following its expansion in April 2024, and the Ministry of Finance confirmed in August 2024 that LGBTQ people may open joint bank accounts and name partners as beneficiaries without restriction.

Residents face the same 2024 criminal-code position as visitors: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita omits the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences carried by the Indian Penal Code it replaced.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was reported as pending in late March 2026; the sources do not confirm whether assent has since been given, and the operative text should be verified against the statute as enacted.

No source in this inventory documents Arunāchal Pradesh-specific facilities, welfare boards, police conduct or hospital capacity for trans people. State-level examples cited here (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra, Odisha) come from other states and are illustrative of the national pattern, not evidence about Arunāchal Pradesh.

Police-conduct assessments conflict: a foreign government's December 2025 policy note describes abuse as limited and non-systemic, while June 2024 victim interviews document abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The inventory does not resolve which picture applies in Arunāchal Pradesh.

The census figure of 487,803 and the estimate of around two million transgender people in India are drawn from different counting methods and are not reconciled in the sources.
